title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 29
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A council reports that since it introduced a garden waste collection charge, the tonnage of garden waste collected has fallen by 35 per cent. It concludes that residents are composting more at home.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The charge is £40 a year.
B. Some residents subscribed to the service before the charge began.
C. Collections are fortnightly in winter.
D. Reports of garden waste dumped on verges and in woodland have risen sharply since the charge was introduced.
E. Neighbouring councils charge similar amounts.
questions.explanation: Fly-tipping accounts for the missing tonnage without any composting, and it is a worse outcome than the collections the charge displaced.

questions.prompt: A software firm reports that projects using its new planning method finish closer to their estimated dates than projects that do not. Management concludes that the method improves scheduling accuracy.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Teams choose the method for projects whose requirements are already well understood, and use the older approach where the work is exploratory.
B. The method requires a two-day training course.
C. The method was developed internally.
D. Some teams use both methods on different projects.
E. Estimated dates are recorded at the start of each project.
questions.explanation: Predictable projects are assigned the method, so the accuracy difference may exist before the method is applied to anything.

questions.prompt: A city reports that road deaths fell by 20 per cent in the year after it lowered the urban speed limit, and attributes the fall to the new limit.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the attribution?
options: A. How many signs had to be replaced
B. Whether drivers support the lower limit
C. Whether road deaths fell by a similar proportion in comparable cities that did not change their limits
D. How the limit is enforced at night
E. What the previous limit had been
questions.explanation: Road deaths are volatile and fell nationally in many periods; a comparison group separates the policy from the trend.

questions.prompt: A supermarket found that customers who use its mobile app spend 30 per cent more per month than customers who do not, and plans to push all customers to install the app in order to raise spending.
questions.question: The plan assumes which of the following?
options: A. The app is free to download.
B. Customers carry mobile telephones while shopping.
C. The app will not increase the chain's costs.
D. Rival chains do not have apps.
E. The spending difference reflects the app's effect rather than the habits of customers who choose to install it.
questions.explanation: Frequent, committed shoppers install a supermarket's app; installing it for occasional shoppers need not make them frequent.

questions.prompt: Every train on the Melbury line that carries a buffet car is formed of eight coaches. No eight-coach train has been cancelled for crew shortage this month. Some trains on the line have been cancelled for crew shortage this month.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Buffet cars prevent cancellations.
B. Some trains on the line do not carry a buffet car.
C. Most trains are formed of eight coaches.
D. Eight-coach trains carry more passengers.
E. Crew shortages occur mainly at weekends.
questions.explanation: Cancelled trains are not eight-coach, and carrying a buffet car implies eight coaches, so the cancelled trains carry no buffet car. B asserts a causal link the premises do not support.

questions.prompt: A charity reports that its donors who give monthly by direct debit contribute more over five years than donors who give occasional single gifts, and proposes to convert all occasional donors to monthly giving.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the proposal?
options: A. Direct debits are cheaper to administer.
B. Some monthly donors cancel within a year.
C. The charity has 40,000 donors.
D. Occasional donors who are pressed to commit monthly frequently give a small monthly sum in place of the larger single gifts they had been making.
E. Monthly giving is promoted by other charities.
questions.explanation: Substitution can lower total income from that group even though monthly donors, as a class, give more — the comparison does not transfer to a conversion.

questions.prompt: An employer notes that staff who take their full annual leave entitlement receive better performance ratings than staff who do not, and concludes that taking leave improves performance.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Leave must be booked a month in advance.
B. Staff who are struggling with their workload postpone leave in order to catch up, and their difficulties are what the ratings reflect.
C. The company offers 25 days of leave.
D. Ratings are given annually by line managers.
E. Some staff carry leave over to the next year.
questions.explanation: The direction of causation is reversed: poor performance prevents leave rather than the absence of leave causing poor performance.

questions.prompt: A publisher argues that its new cover design increased sales, citing that the reissued edition sold more copies in its first month than the original edition sold in its first month five years earlier.
questions.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. does not state the price of either edition
B. ignores the cost of the redesign
C. compares two periods without accounting for the author's reputation having grown in the intervening years
D. relies on figures for a single month
E. assumes readers notice cover designs
questions.explanation: A reissue benefits from an established author and an existing readership; the comparison confounds the cover with five years of accumulated reputation.

questions.prompt: A hospital trust introduced a discharge checklist and reports that readmissions within 30 days fell by 12 per cent. A researcher wishes to establish whether the checklist caused the fall.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the causal claim?
options: A. The checklist was introduced ward by ward over eighteen months, and readmissions fell in each ward only after that ward adopted it.
B. Staff report that the checklist is easy to use.
C. The trust also refurbished two wards during the period.
D. Readmission rates fell nationally over the same period.
E. The checklist has 14 items.
questions.explanation: Staggered adoption ties the effect to the treatment in both time and place, which is what C and D would otherwise undermine.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer of water filters advertises that its product removes 99% of a named contaminant, citing laboratory tests.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advertisement's implication for household use?
options: A. The tests were conducted by an independent laboratory.
B. The contaminant is present in most tap water.
C. The filter must be replaced every six months.
D. Competing filters make similar claims.
E. The laboratory tests used water at a flow rate a quarter of that in a domestic tap, and removal falls sharply at household flow rates.
questions.explanation: The claim may be true under the conditions tested and false under the conditions of use, which is what the advertisement implies.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to make cycle helmets compulsory argue that helmets reduce head injuries. Opponents reply that in cities where helmets were made compulsory, cycling fell sharply and the health benefits of cycling were lost.
questions.question: The opponents' reply is best described as
options: A. denying that helmets reduce head injuries
B. questioning the accuracy of injury statistics
C. claiming that helmets cause accidents
D. arguing that the policy has a cost the supporters' evidence does not measure
E. proposing that cycle lanes be built instead
questions.explanation: The reply concedes the protective effect per cyclist and points to an effect on the number of cyclists, which a study of injuries among cyclists cannot capture.

questions.passageText:
A firm that trains a worker in skills usable elsewhere faces a problem it cannot solve alone: the trained worker becomes more valuable to competitors, who did not pay for the training and can offer more. The standard prediction follows that firms will underinvest in general skills and will train only in what is specific to themselves.

Observed behaviour is more varied. Firms in some countries train extensively in transferable skills, and the explanations turn on what stops the poaching. Where wages are compressed by collective agreement, a trained worker's pay rises by less than their productivity, so the training firm keeps part of the return and a rival gains less by hiring them away. Where employers coordinate through an industry body, poaching carries a reputational cost that an individual firm's calculation would ignore. And where a qualification is certified externally, the worker can prove the skill anywhere — which should make poaching easier, and in practice accompanies more training rather than less, because it also lets the trainee accept lower pay during training in exchange for a credential.

The awkward implication is that the arrangements which make training work look, from inside a single firm, like restrictions. Wage compression is a constraint on paying the best workers what they are worth; an employers' body that penalises poaching is a limit on competition for staff. Each is a cost to the firm and a condition of the system's output, which is why reforms that free firms individually have sometimes reduced training in aggregate — an outcome no participant intended and none could prevent alone.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the standard prediction about training holds that firms will
options: A. train extensively in transferable skills
B. refuse to train workers at all
C. underinvest in general skills and train only in what is specific to them
D. pay trained workers their full productivity
E. rely on external certification
questions.explanation: The poaching problem gives the firm no way to capture the return on general skills, so the prediction is underinvestment in exactly those.

questions.passageTitle: Testing a Theory in an Eclipse
questions.passageText:
The 1919 eclipse expeditions are remembered as the moment general relativity was confirmed by observation. The episode is more instructive when the evidence is examined rather than the story.

The prediction was specific: light passing close to the Sun should be deflected by an amount twice what Newtonian physics implied. An eclipse makes the test possible by allowing stars near the Sun's edge to be photographed, and their apparent positions compared with photographs of the same field taken months earlier.

The measurement was at the limit of what the equipment could do. The deflection is under two seconds of arc; plates expand and contract with temperature; one instrument gave results so scattered that its data were set aside. The decision to exclude that instrument has been argued about ever since, and the honest summary is that the exclusion was defensible on grounds stated at the time and also convenient for the result obtained.

What settles the matter is not the 1919 data but what followed: radio interferometry, repeated eclipse measurements with better instruments, and eventually the tracking of spacecraft signals passing near the Sun, all agreeing with the prediction to precisions the original expeditions could not approach. The correct reading of 1919 is therefore not that one observation proved a theory, but that a marginal result pointed in a direction later confirmed by measurements strong enough to stand alone — and that the fame of the episode rests on the announcement rather than on the strength of the evidence announced.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the prediction tested in 1919 was that light passing near the Sun would be deflected by
options: A. twice the amount Newtonian physics implied
B. the same amount Newtonian physics implied
C. an amount too small to measure
D. an amount depending on the observer's position
E. half the amount Newtonian physics implied
questions.explanation: The doubling is what made the test discriminating between the two accounts.

questions.passageText:
A bank holds deposits repayable on demand and lends them out for years. The arrangement is useful and inherently fragile: if enough depositors ask for their money at once, a solvent bank fails, and the belief that others will withdraw is reason enough to withdraw. Deposit insurance addresses this directly. If deposits are guaranteed, the reason to run disappears, and runs on insured deposits have been rare wherever the guarantee is credible.

The cost is a change in who bears risk. A depositor who cannot lose money has no reason to ask what the bank does with it, and a bank that can raise insured funds regardless of how it lends them faces weaker discipline from its own creditors. The insurance that removes the run also removes the monitoring, and the response has been supervision and capital requirements — rules substituting for the scrutiny the guarantee displaced.

Two design questions follow and are frequently confused. The first is the limit: a guarantee covering every deposit removes all depositor discipline, while one covering small deposits protects those least able to assess a bank and leaves large depositors with a reason to look. The second is who pays: premiums charged to banks, if flat, make prudent banks subsidise risky ones, so premiums are increasingly risk-based, which requires measuring the risk that the scheme exists because nobody could measure.

The system is therefore a set of trade-offs rather than a solution, and the recurring failure is to treat the absence of runs as evidence that the underlying fragility has been removed rather than transferred.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that a bank run can occur at a solvent bank because
options: A. depositors are legally entitled to interest
B. the belief that others will withdraw is itself a reason to withdraw
C. supervisors require immediate repayment
D. loans can be recalled at short notice
E. deposit insurance is unavailable
questions.explanation: The fragility is structural: deposits are repayable on demand while the lending is long-term.

questions.passageText:
Printed conversations with named individuals, presented as a record of what was said, are a nineteenth-century invention. Before that, newspapers reported events and opinions, but the practice of publishing a person's spoken answers under their own name was unusual enough to require explanation when it appeared.

Its arrival depended on several things at once: shorthand rapid enough to capture speech, the telegraph, which made timeliness valuable, and a readership interested in personality as well as event. Early interviews were criticised on grounds that now sound unfamiliar — that they were an intrusion, that a public figure's considered writing was the proper record of their views, and that the form flattered the subject by giving them unmediated space.

The criticism contained a real observation. An interview is a negotiated document. The subject controls what is said, the interviewer controls what is asked and what survives editing, and the resulting text is a joint product presented as one person's speech. That is not a defect to be corrected but the nature of the form, and readers who treat a published interview as transcription misread it.

The convention has since spread far beyond journalism, into recruitment, broadcasting and research, carrying its assumptions with it: that spoken answers under questioning reveal something that written statements do not, and that the person answering is the authority on their own case. Both assumptions are defensible and neither is obvious, which is why the form's history is worth knowing to anyone who relies on it.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, early interviews were criticised on all of the following grounds EXCEPT that they
options: A. were an intrusion
B. displaced considered writing as the record of a person's views
C. were inaccurate as transcription of speech
D. flattered the subject with unmediated space
E. required shorthand and the telegraph
questions.explanation: The three criticisms named are intrusion, the primacy of written statements and flattery. Shorthand and telegraphy are listed as enabling conditions, not complaints, and accuracy of transcription is not among the objections given.

Printed conversations with named individuals, presented as a record of what was said, are a nineteenth-century invention. Before that, newspapers reported events and opinions, but the practice of publishing a person's spoken answers under their own name was unusual enough to require explanation when it appeared.

Its arrival depended on several things at once: shorthand rapid enough to capture speech, the telegraph, which made timeliness valuable, and a readership interested in personality as well as event. Early interviews were criticised on grounds that now sound unfamiliar — that they were an intrusion, that a public figure's considered writing was the proper record of their views, and that the form flattered the subject by giving them unmediated space.

The criticism contained a real observation. An interview is a negotiated document. The subject controls what is said, the interviewer controls what is asked and what survives editing, and the resulting text is a joint product presented as one person's speech. That is not a defect to be corrected but the nature of the form, and readers who treat a published interview as transcription misread it.

The convention has since spread far beyond journalism, into recruitment, broadcasting and research, carrying its assumptions with it: that spoken answers under questioning reveal something that written statements do not, and that the person answering is the authority on their own case. Both assumptions are defensible and neither is obvious, which is why the form's history is worth knowing to anyone who relies on it.
